title: Guadalupe, 1531
hook: Mary appears to Juan Diego near Mexico City and roses fill his cloak in December

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Assumption: Mary taken up, body and soul. Your line was the body matters. Remember the woman clothed with the sun? She's back today.

December, 1531, ten years after the Spanish conquered the Aztec capital. The old world of the Mexica people has been shattered: by war, by disease, by strangers who don't speak their language. On a cold Saturday morning, an Indigenous man named Juan Diego is walking to Mass past a hill called Tepeyac, just outside what's now Mexico City. He hears singing, like birds, but more beautiful. Then a voice calls him by name, tenderly, the way you'd call a child. At the top of the hill stands a young woman, shining.
screen: `TEN YEARS AFTER THE CONQUEST.` → `A HILL CALLED TEPEYAC.` → `A VOICE CALLS HIS NAME.`

segments.voice: The story was later written down in Nahuatl, Juan Diego's own language. The woman speaks to him in Nahuatl too, not Spanish. She tells him she is the Virgin Mary, and asks him to ask the bishop for a church on that hill. The bishop, a Spanish friar, is kind but skeptical: bring me a sign. Meanwhile Juan Diego's uncle falls deathly ill. Going for a priest, he takes the long way around the hill, trying to avoid her. He's embarrassed. He's failed. And she comes down and meets him on the other path anyway. In the story she says, more or less: don't be afraid. Am I not here, I who am your mother? Your uncle is well. She sends him to the frozen hilltop, where he finds roses blooming in December. He gathers them in his tilma, a rough cloak woven from plant fiber, and opens it before the bishop. The roses fall to the floor. And on the cloth is an image of her: dark-skinned, standing in front of the sun, with the moon under her feet. Devotees see in her face and dress a woman of his own people. That cloak hangs today in the Basilica of Guadalupe in Mexico City. Historians debate the early records, and the Church doesn't require anyone to believe in any apparition. Devotion to her runs deep: the Church honors her as patroness of the Americas, and Juan Diego was declared a saint in 2002.
screen: `SHE SPOKE IN NAHUATL.` · `THE LONG WAY AROUND THE HILL.` · `ROSES IN DECEMBER.` · `AN IMAGE ON THE TILMA.` · then, large: `AM I NOT HERE, I WHO AM YOUR MOTHER?`

segments.voice: Picture the map of the Americas, from Alaska to the tip of Chile, and let faces come one by one: a migrant on a long road, a grandmother in a village, a kid in a big city, a family you know. If you pray, ask Our Lady of Guadalupe to be near them, the way she was near a tired man who took the long way around. If you don't pray, simply wish them well.
Guadalupe. Mary as she appeared, the story says, to Juan Diego in 1531, speaking his own language, roses in his cloak. Today's word.
Your line: she spoke his language. And she met him on the path he took to avoid her. Day eighty-three, done.

howItsDone: Catholics celebrate Our Lady of Guadalupe on 12 December, when great crowds of pilgrims visit her basilica in Mexico City; Saint Juan Diego's day is 9 December.

sources.ref: John Paul II, canonization of Juan Diego (31 July 2002); Ecclesia in America 11 (1999)

notes: The apparition story follows the Nican Mopohua (attributed to Antonio Valeriano; published by Luis Laso de la Vega, 1649). 'Am I not here, I who am your mother?' is a paraphrase of the Nahuatl, deliberately without quotation marks, as modern translations are copyrighted.
Dates: first apparition 9 December 1531; tilma shown to Bishop Juan de Zumárraga 12 December. Confirm.
Historical debate: early Spanish documents (including Zumárraga's) do not mention the apparition; the script says 'historians debate the early records'. Keeper should confirm the tone is right.
Image details (brown-skinned, dressed like a noblewoman, before the sun, moon under her feet) described in general terms; confirm.
Patroness of the Americas: Pius XII (1945/46); John Paul II in Ecclesia in America (1999). Juan Diego canonized 31 July 2002. Confirm.
The conquest (fall of Tenochtitlan, 1521) is named honestly without drama; confirm framing.
games.original is null: Nahuatl terms are written in Latin script and none was judged worth a pronunciation card.
